title: Declining physical activity
prompt: Many people in modern societies do less physical activity than previous generations, which is contributing to a rise in health problems. What are the main causes of this trend, and what solutions could be introduced?

sentences.text: Across many countries, people spend longer sitting at desks, in cars and in front of screens than they did a generation ago.
sentences.why: Neutral background that frames the trend through three concrete places: "desks, cars and screens". The contrast with "a generation ago" paraphrases "previous generations" and sets the topic, supporting Lexical Resource and Task Response.

sentences.text: This shift has several causes, and I believe the most effective solutions combine changes to urban design with support in the workplace.
sentences.why: A thesis that previews both parts: "several causes" and "most effective solutions". It names the two solution types, which sets up a logical match with the causes and shows organised, precise planning for Task Response.

sentences.text: This essay will examine the main causes of inactivity and then suggest two practical responses.
sentences.why: The outline states the order of the essay in two steps. "Causes ... then ... two practical responses" is a clear roadmap, and "practical" signals a realistic approach, which supports Coherence and Cohesion.

sentences.text: The most significant cause is the growing dependence on cars and sedentary jobs, which removes everyday movement from people's lives.
sentences.why: A topic sentence naming the main cause and its effect: "removes everyday movement". "Most significant" ranks the cause, and the noun phrase "dependence on cars and sedentary jobs" is precise, supporting Lexical Resource.

sentences.text: When short journeys are made by car, and office work involves hours of sitting, the body receives far less exercise than it would from walking or manual labour.
sentences.why: Explains the mechanism with a contrast between sitting and "walking or manual labour". The "When ... and ..." clause structure sets up the condition, and "far less exercise" quantifies the result, giving range.

sentences.text: In many suburban areas, for instance, shops and schools are too far away to reach on foot, so residents drive even for brief errands.
sentences.why: A relevant, familiar example: suburbs where "shops and schools are too far". "Even for brief errands" shows how deep the dependence is, and "for instance" signals the example, supporting believable development.

sentences.text: Over time, this lack of movement contributes to obesity, heart disease and weaker bone health.
sentences.why: The effect sentence lists health outcomes tied back to the question. "Over time" gives a time frame and "contributes to" is a measured cause verb, avoiding overclaiming. It closes the paragraph with a clear consequence.

sentences.text: One practical solution is to redesign towns so that walking and cycling are safer and more convenient.
sentences.why: A topic sentence that links directly to the cause: "redesign towns" answers car dependence. "Safer and more convenient" gives the two conditions for success, so the solution has an aim, supporting Task Response.

sentences.text: Protected cycle lanes, well-lit pavements and local services within walking distance make active travel a realistic choice rather than an occasional one.
sentences.why: Explains how the design works with a triple list of features, and "a realistic choice rather than an occasional one" contrasts types of behaviour. It shows the mechanism, not only the measure.

sentences.text: Where segregated cycle routes have been built in several European cities, cycling has grown noticeably among commuters.
sentences.why: Provides evidence of effectiveness: "segregated cycle routes ... several European cities" and "grown noticeably". The adverbial "Where ..." clause is a conditional-like structure and the hedge is accurate, supporting credibility.

sentences.text: Employers can complement this by offering standing desks, walking meetings and incentives for active travel, which encourage movement during the working day.
sentences.why: The second solution is added with "complement", showing how the measures work together. Listing "standing desks, walking meetings and incentives" is concrete, and the final relative clause explains the purpose.

sentences.text: In short, inactivity stems largely from car-based lifestyles and sedentary work, and it can be reduced through better urban planning and workplace policies.
sentences.why: The conclusion restates both causes and both solutions in new words: "stems largely from" and "better urban planning and workplace policies". It confirms that the solutions match the causes, giving Coherence and a full answer.

sentences.text: Without such changes, the health burden of inactivity will continue to grow, so these measures should be treated as a priority.
sentences.why: A final judgement that gives a consequence of inaction with "Without such changes". "Health burden" is a precise collocation and "priority" gives an action, so it closes the essay without introducing new ideas.

analysis: The question words are "what are the main causes" and "what solutions could be introduced". Two separate answers are required, so each needs its own developed paragraph.
The problem is declining physical activity linked to health problems. Causes must explain why people move less, not simply restate the health consequences, and solutions must reduce inactivity.
Paraphrase in the introduction: "do less physical activity" becomes lead more sedentary lives; "previous generations" becomes a generation ago; "rise in health problems" becomes growing health risks.
Choose one main cause and link it to a solution: car dependence and sedentary jobs lead to town redesign and workplace measures. This match is what examiners reward at Band 7 and above.
Solutions need an agent and a mechanism: local authorities building cycle lanes, and employers offering standing desks and incentives. "People should exercise more" is not a solution.
The question is not asking for a history of lifestyle change or a discussion of whether inactivity is the individual's fault. Keep to causes and solutions.

plan.idea: People sit for longer than a generation ago. Thesis: several causes, and the best solutions combine urban design with workplace support.
Main cause: dependence on cars and sedentary jobs removes everyday movement. Example: suburbs where shops and schools are too far to walk. Result: obesity, heart disease, weaker bones.
Solution 1: redesign towns with protected cycle lanes, lit pavements and local services; evidence from European cities. Solution 2: employers add standing desks, walking meetings and incentives.
Inactivity stems from car-based lifestyles and sedentary work and can be reduced by planning and workplace policy; without change the health burden will grow.
